newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: British hostage escapes from Khmer Rouge-official.
newsitem.headline: British hostage escapes from Khmer Rouge-official.

text.p: British mine-clearance expert Christopher Howes and his Cambodian interpreter escaped from Khmer Rouge captivity earlier this month and are expected to arrive in Phnom Penh on Friday, a top military official said.
The two men were abducted in the northwest province of Siem Reap on March 26.

They escaped from the Khmer Rouge base at Anlong Veng near the Thai border on November 5 with the help of their guards and guerrilla defectors, the armed forces deputy chief of staff, Lieutenant General Nhiek Bun Chhay, told reporters on Thursday.

The two men, members of the UK-based Mines Advisory Group (MAG), reached Anlong Kranh village in central Kompong Thom province in the company of their Khmer Rouge guards and defectors, Nhiek Bun Chhay said after stepping off a helicopter from Kompong Thom.
"There were 151 separatists led by a division commander and including Howes's 11 guards," he said. "They helped him escape from Anlong Veng."
"It took a long time because there were problems in travelling," the general said of the tough journey from Anlong Veng to Anlong Kranh, some 185 km (115 miles) north of Phnom Penh.
The British Embassy and the MAG office in Phnom Penh said they had not received confirmation that Howes was free, and were investigating the reports.

Nhiek Bun Chhay said he had not seen Howes, 36, and his interpreter, Houn Hourth, but had been told by radio that they were thin but healthy. He expected them to be flown to Phnom Penh on Friday afternoon.

"I don't know why they didn't kill him, but he was ordered to work hard during the day and put in prison at night," the general said, adding that the Briton had escaped with one hand in a handcuff after being cut free.
Howes, a supervisor with the group that had helped clear mines in Kuwait and Iraq, had been forced to spend much of his time teaching the Khmer Rouge around Anlong Veng how to make mines.

There have been mixed reports over the past few months about the fate of the two men, who were among a large group of MAG mine clearers abducted not far from the famed Angkor temples, a tourist attraction.

MAG closed its Siem Reap operation after the abductions but maintains operations in Kompong Thom and the western province of Battambang with 260 Cambodian mine-clearers and three British technical advisers.

In August, the Bangkok Post said Howes had been executed in Anlong Veng and that Houn Hourth died of malaria in July. But a breakaway Khmer Rouge commander said in October that Howes was still alive in captivity.

Nominal Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Samphan earlier this month responded to a request from King Norodom Sihanouk for information about Howes and Houn Hourth by saying the guerrilla faction had nothing to do with their abduction.
The Khmer Rouge, who ruled Cambodia by terror during Pol Pot's 1975-79 "killing fields" rule, had been fighting the coalition government that emerged from U.N.-supervised general elections in 1993.
The Maoist group has kidnapped more than a dozen Westerners since the coalition was formed and killed at least seven of them.

The movement has been savaged by an internal split and massive defections since August, when former top official Ieng Sary broke with the hardliners at Anlong Veng and opened peace negotiations with the government.
